Frontier Architecture & Reasoning · Part 1 · Snapshot: September 2026 🧬

Frontier Model Research & Innovation: What's Changing Inside the Models

The frontier is no longer "a bigger dense transformer". Today's leading models activate a small slice of a huge network per token, attend to a million tokens with compressed and sparse attention, think longer when a problem is hard, see and hear natively, reason about the physical world, and are shaped by reinforcement learning on verifiable goals. This visual deep dive explains each shift with interactive diagrams — and grounds each in a publicly documented 2026 model.

How to read this: every diagram is interactive — move the sliders and press the buttons; the numbers they show are computed from the stated formulas, not decorative. Claims about specific models come from their technical reports, model cards and API documentation, linked in References, as of September 2026. Where a lab doesn't disclose a detail (most don't disclose parameter counts), we say so rather than guess.

01 The Big Picture: Beyond a Dense, Next-Token Transformer

Until about 2023, progress mostly meant a larger dense transformer trained on more data: every parameter used for every token, one forward pass per output token. Frontier models now improve along many dimensions at once, and parameter count is only one of them.

2023-style dense model
2026 frontier model

A conceptual comparison, not measured scores: each axis is a dimension along which frontier models now improve, and the purple shape grows along all of them — not just "size".

The frontier is shifting from "bigger dense models" to "smarter, more capable and more efficient model architectures and training methods."

02 Mixture-of-Experts and Sparse Activation

A Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) layer replaces the transformer's single feed-forward network with many smaller "experts" and a router that sends each token to just a few of them. The model can have a huge total parameter count while each token only pays for the experts it uses. The idea goes back to Shazeer et al.'s sparsely-gated MoE (2017); Switch Transformer routed each token to one expert, Mixtral 8×7B to two of eight, and DeepSeek's models use many small fine-grained experts plus always-on shared experts.

▶ Watch the router Each token is scored by the router, which activates only its top-k experts.
What the router does
Scores every expert for the current token, keeps the top-k, and mixes their outputs weighted by those scores. Experts tend to specialize (for example on code, mathematics or particular languages), though specialization is emergent rather than assigned.
Why load balancing matters
If the router favours a few experts, they overload and others never learn. Training adds balancing pressure — auxiliary losses in Switch and Mixtral, and an auxiliary-loss-free bias adjustment in DeepSeek-V3 — so experts are used evenly.
Documented example — DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash (September 2026): 552B total parameters, about 8B active per token while processing input and 16B while generating output (DeepSeek technical report). Earlier: DeepSeek-V3 used 671B total with 37B active; DeepSeek-V4-Pro 1.6T total with 49B active; Google describes Gemini 3 Pro as a sparse mixture-of-experts transformer without publishing sizes.

03 Efficient Attention and Long Context

Standard attention compares every token with every earlier token, so its cost grows with the square of the context length — and its memory (the KV cache) grows linearly with every token kept. A million-token context needs different attention patterns and compressed memory. The diagram shows which query–key pairs each pattern computes:

▶ Attention patterns Rows are queries (tokens being produced), columns are keys (tokens attended to). Coloured cells are computed.
TechniqueIdeaExamples
Sliding-window attentionEach token attends only to the last w tokens: cost grows linearlyLongformer, Mistral 7B, local layers in many hybrids
Hybrid local + globalMix cheap local layers with occasional full-attention layersMany 2025–26 open models
Sparse (selected) attentionA lightweight indexer picks the most relevant earlier tokens; attend only to thoseDeepSeek Sparse Attention (Lightning Indexer + top-k)
Compressed KVStore fewer, smaller key/value entries: grouped heads, low-rank latents, pooling several tokens into one, low-precision cachesGQA; DeepSeek MLA; DeepSeek-V4 compressed sparse attention; FP4 KV in V4.1-Flash
Context parallelismSplit a very long sequence across GPUs during training and prefillRing attention, Llama 3 context parallelism
▶ How big is a million-token memory? KV-cache size for one sequence, from each model's per-token footprint.
Per-token footprints: a Llama-3-70B-shaped model with grouped-query attention stores 2 × 80 layers × 8 KV heads × 128 dims × 2 bytes = 327,680 bytes per token (computed). DeepSeek reports a global KV footprint of 890 bytes per token for V4.1-Flash, about a quarter of V4-Flash's (so ~3,560 bytes, derived). Real deployments add paging and other overheads.
Documented example — DeepSeek-V4 (April 2026): a hybrid of compressed sparse attention (pooling several tokens' keys and values into one entry, then selecting the most relevant with DeepSeek Sparse Attention, plus a sliding window for local detail) and heavily compressed attention. At a one-million-token context, DeepSeek reports V4-Pro needs 27% of the per-token inference FLOPs and 10% of the KV cache of DeepSeek-V3.2.

04 Reasoning via RL and Test-Time Compute

Two linked ideas turned "chatbots" into reasoning models. First, reinforcement learning on problems with checkable answers teaches a model to produce long chains of reasoning that end in correct answers. Second, test-time compute: spending more computation at inference — thinking longer, sampling several solutions, verifying and choosing — buys accuracy on hard problems. Snell et al. (2024) found that allocating test-time compute adaptively per problem can be over four times more efficient than simple best-of-N sampling.

▶ Sample, verify, select If one attempt is right with probability p, how often does the system get it right with N attempts?
Computed exactly: a perfect verifier succeeds if any attempt is right, 1 − (1 − p)N. Majority vote (self-consistency) succeeds if the right answer is the most common one; here wrong answers are assumed to be spread over 4 distinct alternatives. Real verifiers are imperfect, and attempts are correlated, so real gains are smaller — but the shape holds: verification beats voting, and both cost N times the compute.

Methods range from self-consistency (sample several chains, take the majority answer) and best-of-N with a reward model or verifier, to process reward models that score each reasoning step (Lightman et al.'s "Let's Verify Step by Step" found step-level supervision beat outcome-only supervision on MATH), to parallel thinking that explores several hypotheses and combines them. It raises latency and cost, which is why it has to be controllable (next section).

Documented example — Gemini Deep Think: an advanced version of Gemini with Deep Think, which uses parallel thinking, reached the gold-medal standard at the 2025 International Mathematical Olympiad, solving five of six problems (35/42) end to end in natural language. Google upgraded Gemini 3 Deep Think in February 2026 for scientific, research and engineering problems.

05 Adaptive and Controllable Thinking

Thinking longer isn't always worth it: an easy question answered after a long deliberation is just slow and expensive. Modern models let the caller set a thinking budget, and let the model adapt its effort — stopping early when confident, thinking longer on hard problems.

▶ Thinking budget Same question, three thinking levels. Illustrative token counts.
Documented example — Gemini 3.7 Flash (August 2026): Google's developer documentation exposes a thinking_level setting with values LOW, MEDIUM (the default) and HIGH; LOW is recommended for latency-critical tasks such as real-time chat, HIGH for complex reasoning, hard mathematics and difficult coding or agent tasks. The trade-off it controls is quality against latency and cost.

06 Native Multimodality

Early multimodal systems bolted a vision encoder onto a finished language model. Natively multimodal models are trained from the start on interleaved text, images, audio and video, so every modality becomes tokens in one shared sequence and one transformer reasons over all of them.

▶ Many modalities, one token stream Each input is encoded into tokens and interleaved into a single sequence.
📝 Text
🖼️ Image
🎙️ Audio
🎬 Video
💻 Code / data
→ tokenizers & encoders →
→ one shared transformer →
text · images · audio

Benefits: cross-modal understanding (answer a question about a chart inside a video), generation across modalities, and reasoning that mixes them. Costs: images, audio and video produce many tokens, which is part of why efficient long context matters so much.

Documented examples: Google's model card describes Gemini 3.1 Pro as natively multimodal, taking text, audio, images, video and entire code repositories in a context of up to one million tokens, with up to 64K output tokens. DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash trains its vision encoder from scratch, processing visual embeddings jointly with text from the start of pretraining.

07 Embodied and Physical Reasoning

Embodied reasoning connects perception to action in the physical world: understanding 3D space, physical properties and causality, reasoning over time, and planning actions a robot can execute. A common split: a reasoning model ("the brain") understands the scene and plans, and a vision-language-action (VLA) model turns each step into motor commands.

▶ The perception-to-action loop Press play to run one cycle.
Task: “Put the cup in the sink.”
Documented example — Gemini Robotics ER 2 (July 2026): Google DeepMind's embodied-reasoning model, built on Gemini 3.5 Flash, acts as a high-level "brain": it understands scenes and continuous video, tracks task progress, plans multi-step tasks and coordinates multiple robots, then hands motor execution to a lower-level VLA model. It is available to developers through the Gemini API.

08 Post-Training Innovation for Reasoning

Beyond next-token pretraining, a growing share of a model's reasoning ability now comes from post-training. The ladder:

Supervised fine-tuningLearn from high-quality demonstrations
Reinforcement learningReward outcomes: correct answers, task success
Verifiable rewardsAutomatic checkers for maths, code and logic — no human labels needed
Process supervisionReward good intermediate steps, not just final answers
Self-generated problemsModels create harder training tasks for themselves
Tool use & agent experienceTrain on real and simulated tool interactions

A key algorithm is GRPO (Group Relative Policy Optimization), used for DeepSeek-R1. Instead of training a separate value model, it samples a group of answers to the same prompt, scores each with a verifiable reward, and pushes up answers that beat the group average:

▶ GRPO: a group of answers, scored against each other Click answers to toggle correct / wrong and watch the advantages.
Advantage of answer i = (rewardi − mean) ÷ standard deviation of the group's rewards, computed live. Correct answers get positive advantages (made more likely), wrong ones negative. If every answer scores the same, all advantages are zero — the group teaches nothing — which is why training uses problems of the right difficulty.
Documented example — DeepSeek-R1 (Nature, September 2025): DeepSeek-R1-Zero was trained from the DeepSeek-V3 base with GRPO and rule-based rewards (answer accuracy and format) and no supervised fine-tuning first; self-verification, reflection and longer reasoning emerged during training. See How Post-Training Works for SFT, RLHF and DPO in depth.

09 Distillation and Model Efficiency

Distillation trains a smaller student to imitate a larger teacher — not only its final answers but its full probability distributions (Hinton et al., 2015) or its reasoning traces. The teacher's "soft" probabilities carry more information than a single correct label: which wrong answers are nearly right.

▶ Soft targets and temperature The teacher's scores for the next word after “The cat sat on the …”. Raise the temperature to reveal what it knows about the alternatives.
Probabilities = softmax(logit ÷ T), computed live from fixed example logits. At T = 1 the teacher is nearly certain; at higher T the student also learns that “sofa” is far more plausible than “moon”.

Related efficiency work: multi-token prediction (training a model to predict several future tokens at once — used in DeepSeek-V3 and useful for faster speculative decoding), architecture-aware distillation into smaller dense or MoE models, and asymmetric compute. DeepSeek-R1's reasoning was also distilled into smaller open Qwen- and Llama-based models.

Documented example — asymmetric compute in DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash: a “causal encoder–decoder” design activates about 8B parameters per token when processing input (prefill) and 16B when generating output (decode), because agent workloads read far more tokens than they write.

10 Emerging Architecture Directions

⚖️
Asymmetric compute

Different compute for reading input and writing output (DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash).

🪜
Adaptive depth

Spend a different number of layers per token; Mixture-of-Depths routes easy tokens around blocks.

🧠
Memory-augmented models

External or learned long-term memory beyond the context window.

〰️
State-space & hybrids

Linear-time sequence layers (Mamba) mixed with attention (Jamba and others) for long inputs.

🎯
New training objectives

Beyond next-token prediction: multi-token prediction, world models, contrastive and verifiable objectives.

🔩
Efficient architectures

Better parameterization, low-precision (FP8/FP4) training and inference, quantization-aware training.

These are active research directions. No single new architecture has replaced the transformer; several are producing strong results, often as hybrids with it.

2024DeepSeek-V2 introduces multi-head latent attention; DeepSeek-V3 (Dec) — 671B MoE, 37B active, multi-token prediction
2025DeepSeek-R1 (Jan): reasoning from RL with verifiable rewards; Gemini Deep Think reaches IMO gold (Jul); Gemini 3 (Nov)
2026Gemini 3 Deep Think upgrade (Feb); DeepSeek-V4 with compressed sparse attention and 1M context (Apr); Gemini Robotics ER 2 (Jul); Gemini 3.7 Flash thinking levels (Aug); DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash (Sep)
✓Less emphasis on parameter count alone; more on active parameters, sparsity and efficiency.
✓Major progress in long context: compressed and sparse attention make a million tokens practical.
✓Reasoning-time scaling became a standard, controllable feature.
✓Native multimodality and embodied reasoning moved from research to products and APIs.
✓More verifiable, process-based training objectives; greater focus on agent and tool competence.

Dense modelsSparse / MoE

The frontier in one paragraph
Frontier models in 2026 get their gains less from raw size and more from how compute is spent: sparse experts so only a small slice of a huge model runs per token; compressed, sparse attention so a million tokens fit in memory; reinforcement learning on verifiable goals plus controllable test-time thinking so hard problems get more computation than easy ones; native multimodality and embodied reasoning so the same model reads, sees, hears and plans actions; and distillation and asymmetric designs so all of it gets cheaper. The transformer is still the core — but the model around it looks very different from 2023's dense next-token predictor.
